title: OX Security Launches OX Radar and Response Center to Show Companies Which Cyber Threats Actually Affect Them
raw_text: New technology monitors critical vulnerabilities and supply chain threats, automatically assessing customer exposure and guiding remediation OX Security , a leader in AI-native application protection, today announced the launch of OX Radar and Response Center, giving security teams one place to track high-priority cyber threats, determine whether their organizations are affected, and manage remediation. OX Radar continuously monitors emerging vulnerabilities, compromised software dependencies, and actively exploited threats. Integrated with OX Security’s application security platform, the Response Center automatically checks supported threats against customer environments, identifying affected assets and providing the context and guidance needed to respond. Separately, a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed provides broader security research and findings across the software and AI supply chain. When a major vulnerability or supply chain attack emerges, security teams often spend hours searching advisories, checking inventories, and correlating findings across tools to answer the question that matters most: Are we affected? As new software and AI components proliferate, investigating every potential threat manually is becoming increasingly impractical. “The question isn’t just whether a new threat is dangerous. It’s whether it’s dangerous to you,” said Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security. “AI is accelerating software development, expanding the supply chain, and generating more security alerts than teams can realistically investigate. Security teams need to know immediately which threats affect their organization, which don’t, and what action is required.” From Breaking Threats to Customer Action To help security teams stay ahead of threats requiring urgent attention, OX Radar scans CVE databases, known-exploited vulnerability catalogs, security advisories, and vendor research approximately every 10 minutes. The customer-facing capabilities focus on high-priority threats, including compromised or malicious dependencies, exploited vulnerabilities, and critical-severity CVEs. The Response Center connects supported OX Radar threats to each customer’s environment, checking whether vulnerable components are present and assessing their exploitability. It combines intelligence from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, EPSS exploit predictions, and VEX exploitability status with OX Security’s AI-generated exploit checks and runtime visibility to determine whether vulnerable libraries are affected. Through the Response Center, security teams can: Track threats: Follow high-priority incidents as new intelligence and findings emerge. Assess exposure: Identify affected assets and examine supporting evidence. Prioritize risk: Evaluate severity, exploitation, code usage, and reachability. Manage remediation: Access safe versions and guidance, and create or track tickets and fix pull requests. Document response: Maintain records of findings and remediation activity. For each supported incident, the Response Center indicates whether a vulnerability has been detected in the customer’s environment, provides evidence of its potential exploitability, and incorporates available VEX information to help teams determine whether action is required. Teams can also initiate investigations using a CVE identifier, GitHub Security Advisory identifier, or advisory URL. Expanding Threat Visibility Through Public Research Alongside the customer-facing capabilities, OX Security is introducing a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed with a broader catalog of security findings. Powered by OX Security’s independent research and scanning, the feed analyzes newly published npm and PyPI packages, AI skills, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. OX Security will continue expanding the range of threats assessed against customer environments, bringing more findings from its public research into the Response Center over time. Availability OX Radar and Response Center are available to OX Security customers as part of OX Security’s AI-Native Application Protection Platform (AINAPP). The broader OX Radar research feed is publicly accessible through the OX Security website. About OX Security OX Security is the first AI-Native Application Protection Platform built to secure software from prompt to production runtime. Its platform includes VibeSec, OX Code, OX Cloud, and OX Agentic Pentester, giving security teams a unified system for securing AI-driven development, applications, and cloud environments. Contact Head of Communications Jillian Jones OX Security jillian.jones@ox.security
summary: New technology monitors critical vulnerabilities and supply chain threats, automatically assessing customer exposure and guiding remediation OX Security , a leader in AI-native application protection, today announced the launch of OX Radar and Response Center, giving security teams one place to track high-priority cyber threats, determine whether their organizations are affected, and manage remediation. OX Radar continuously monitors emerging vulnerabilities, compromised software dependencies, and actively exploited threats. Integrated with OX Security’s application security platform, the Response Center automatically checks supported threats against customer environments, identifying affected assets and providing the context and guidance needed to respond. Separately, a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed provides broader security research and findings across the software and AI supply chain.

title: Attackers hijack Microsoft’s agent-framework package to steal Azure and CI credentials
raw_text: Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers. Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour. “The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post . The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said. The malicious versions also installed the genuine framework code, so applications kept working, and the compromise was easy to miss. The package has 192,534 monthly downloads, according to the firm. Other security firms, including Aikido Security, Endor Labs, and SafeDep, published similar analyses of the attack. Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. How the stealer worked The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said. It also read up to 60 credential files. These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files. It pulled secrets from up to 300 other running processes as well. The stealer also asked for new tokens. Inside Azure DevOps pipelines, it requested an identity token that can be exchanged for Azure access, OX said in the blog post. It also requested managed identity tokens for Azure services, including Resource Manager, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Cognitive Services, AI Foundry, and Azure DevOps. Endor Labs said the attack was aimed mainly at automated build systems. “Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis . The code was disguised as diagnostics. It sat in a module named _telemetry.py and sent data with a user agent labeled “af-runtime-diagnostics,” OX said. The stolen data went to a webhook.site address as compressed, encoded JSON. The attacker did not stop after the first release. While OX was researching the malware, version 1.26.1 was reverted to the clean 1.26.0. The attacker then uploaded 1.26.2, which used a different file path for the same payload, the firm said. The first version went up at 20:35 UTC and the second at 21:08 UTC, according to Aikido Security . Both were gone by about 21:20 UTC. “This attack isn’t just a one-off exfiltration attempt, but a planned, live and coordinated effort to reach as many victims as they can, while still being able to bypass blocks and restrictions,” OX said. OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files. Endor Labs, in its analysis, said both malicious versions were uploaded as wheel files only, without the source code package that came with the clean release. Microsoft has not confirmed how the breach happened. The short window may not limit exposure. Any unpinned install during that time pulled in a malicious version, Endor Labs said. Container images, CI caches, and lockfiles built in the window could still contain it. AI pipelines in focus OX said the attack shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it. The stealer’s target list includes OpenAI and Hugging Face tokens and Azure AI Foundry access. It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions. No researcher has linked the two attacks. What security teams should do Removing the package does not undo the damage. “Removing the package stops future runs, but it doesn’t undo anything that was already sent,” Aikido said. OX advised teams to check all environments, CI images, and lockfiles for either version and remove it. Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said. Version 1.26.2 used different files, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py, according to Aikido. If the package ran anywhere, every secret reachable from that host should be treated as compromised, OX said. The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens. OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents. Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.
summary: Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers. Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour. “The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post . The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said.

title: The resilience gap: Why cybersecurity investment alone is not enough
raw_text: Death, taxes and cyber incidents. It’s not quite the original saying, but for today’s CISO, all three carry a certain inevitability, and most organizations have come to accept that reality. Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study confirms that cybersecurity remains the top investment priority for CISOs. Yet even well-funded security programs can struggle when something goes wrong. Why? The cause is rarely missing plans or controls; it’s silos. Service owners; security, recovery and crisis teams; and key providers too often plan and operate apart. As a result, organizations are beginning to see that investment and resilience are not the same thing. Ultimately, the investment didn’t fail; the expectation did. Technology alone can’t deliver an outcome that also depends on people, process, governance and coordination. The lesson is clear: A well-funded cybersecurity program can still be operationally fragile. The findings in Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study illustrate the problem. Cybersecurity remains the leading strategic investment priority, selected by 48% of CISOs. Yet only 41% report high or very high confidence in their organizations’ ability to protect enterprise value, while just 29% express that level of confidence in responding with agility. Another 54% describe their confidence in their organizations’ ability to respond with agility as moderate. That gap should concern every CISO. It suggests organizations have built security capabilities without fully developing the enterprise operating model needed during disruption. The real test begins when prevention ends Security investment matters. But you aren’t buying away cyber risk. You’re buying it down. Even the most mature organizations will eventually face an event they cannot prevent, often involving a third party, technology failure or circumstance outside their control. What happens next separates resilient organizations from everyone else. Security works to contain the threat while infrastructure and application teams decide what can safely go offline. Business leaders push to restore critical services, sometimes with competing priorities. Legal weighs disclosure obligations with incomplete information. Communications prepares messages for employees, customers and regulators. Meanwhile, a cloud, software-as-a-service or other technology provider may control part of the environment the company needs to recover. That’s where resilience usually breaks down: not within any one team, but in the handoffs and decisions between them. In the exercises we run, the hardest questions are often surprisingly basic: Who has the authority to shut down a revenue-producing system? If two critical services are down, who decides which comes back first? If Microsoft 365 or another primary collaboration platform is unavailable, how does the crisis team communicate? If a critical provider is also down, do its recovery priorities and timelines align with yours? The useful output of an exercise is not a reassuring score. It is the list of things that didn’t work: unclear authority, gaps in escalation paths, inaccessible backups and dependencies that teams incorrectly assumed had been tested. Consider Quantum Dawn VIII, SIFMA’s sector-wide exercise from November 2025 . The polycrisis scenario included an undersea cable cut, and roughly two-thirds of participants said they had either never tested that scenario or weren’t sure they had. That is exactly the kind of blind spot an exercise is designed to expose. Better to uncover it in an exercise than during an actual disruption. And the event you plan for is seldom the event you get. That’s why resilience cannot depend on following a script. Build a framework that enables collaboration and increases the speed of informed decisions, regardless of what actually happens. Cyber, AI and third-party risks no longer stay in their lanes Risks don’t arrive one at a time. A cyberattack can quickly become a privacy issue, a regulatory matter and a business interruption. A third-party outage becomes your outage. And AI can act as a force multiplier, allowing a single issue to move faster and spread across more data, systems and business processes. The findings support this. Cyber threats remain the highest-rated near-term concern in the Top Risks survey, but privacy, third-party risk, AI, resilience and regulatory uncertainty are now clustered closely behind. AI doesn’t change the fundamental resilience questions. It raises the stakes. An agent may read customer data, query an ERP system, act through a service account or trigger a workflow without a person clicking the button. So, start with an old question: What can it access? Then ask whose permissions or delegated authority it is using, what actions it can take, where those actions are logged and how quickly you can stop it when something goes wrong. CISOs appear to recognize that challenge. In our 2027 Top Risks study, 51% identified improving AI governance and accountability as a leading priority, while 45% pointed to workforce readiness. That’s telling. Sustainable adoption requires some basic discipline: maintain an inventory of agents and their owners, map the data and tools each can reach, restrict service accounts and delegated permissions, monitor actions and make sure access can be revoked quickly. Third parties deserve the same scrutiny. A third-party assessment can tell you a lot about a provider’s controls at a point in time. What it rarely tells you is how that provider will perform on a bad day. Most assessments still rely heavily on documentation, discussion and self-reporting. Those assessments may assure a provider’s security posture, but they do not prove that a critical service will remain available, that the provider’s recovery sequence aligns with yours or that the appropriate people on both sides know how to disconnect, communicate and restore service together. CISOs should be able to identify the external relationships most critical to business operations, understand the services and data that depend on them, and test what will happen if those relationships are interrupted. This broader responsibility is increasingly part of the CISO mandate. CSO’s examination of how CISOs can rise to the business resilience challenge describes the role’s evolution from a primarily preventive function toward greater responsibility for response, recovery and business resilience. Build resilience into the investments already underway If cyber risk increasingly travels through interconnected systems and infrastructure, resilience has to be part of how those environments are modernized in the first place. The percentage of CISOs selecting cybersecurity slipped from 53% to 48%, while the percentage selecting infrastructure modernization rose from 21% to 33%. Taken together, those shifts make sense. Security and modernization are increasingly intertwined. A cloud migration, enterprise resource planning (ERP) replacement, identity redesign or data-platform upgrade can retire unsupported systems and standing privileges. It can also create new concentration risk, recovery dependencies and failure points if resilience is not designed in from the start. CISOs should use these major transformation programs to improve resilience, not complicate it. Questions to ask include: Are we retiring legacy platforms and connections, or simply putting a new layer on top of them? Are old accounts, interfaces, backup jobs and vendor dependencies actually being removed? Can the order-to-cash, payments, customer service or other critical processes be restored faster after the investment? Are recovery, isolation and alternate-processing requirements in the architecture and acceptance criteria from the start? Have we tested the new platform’s recovery path, or are we assuming modernization made it more resilient? Closing the resilience gap The point isn’t to spend less on cybersecurity. It’s to expect more from the investment. The 2027 Top Risks study shows CISOs balancing cyber threats with AI, third-party risk, resilience and modernization. Those may look like separate priorities on a survey. In practice, they increasingly collide in the same incident. We aren’t going to prevent every cyber incident. The question is what happens when the next one gets through. Does the organization know what matters most, who makes the hard calls and how to recover? Or does it figure those things out during the crisis? That gap is the resilience gap. And it is where CISOs should be looking next.
summary: Death, taxes and cyber incidents. It’s not quite the original saying, but for today’s CISO, all three carry a certain inevitability, and most organizations have come to accept that reality. Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study confirms that cybersecurity remains the top investment priority for CISOs. Yet even well-funded security programs can struggle when something goes wrong.

title: How organizations can secure their AI-generated code
raw_text: The IT manager didn’t know the company hired a “vibe coder” straight out of school. By the time they met a few months later, the new hire had already built a web application that operated with customer data and private contracts. The app ran under a domain the new hire controlled, stored data on Supabase’s free plan, and deployed directly from his GitHub repository to Cloudflare’s serverless infrastructure. “He vibe-codes everything straight into production, on servers all over the world,” the IT manager wrote on Reddit . “We’re EU based.” When asked whether he had read the AI-generated code or taken any security precautions, the new hire said, “My GitHub repo is private.” The IT manager took the concern to the CEO, who brushed it aside: “Let it go.” In many organizations, vibe coders build software without thinking much about security. Their apps may get the job done, but they are ticking bombs. In SusVibes , a benchmark of 186 real-world feature requests from open-source projects, agents given feature descriptions without security guidance produced working code up to 57% of the time. But only 11.8% of their solutions were secure. “The failures we saw were not careless errors,” says Danqing Wang of Carnegie Mellon University’s Language Technologies Institute, author of the paper describing SusVibes. “Spotting those requires reasoning about what an attacker can do, not just what the feature should do.” What has changed, especially this year, is that AI code-generating tools have gotten so good at producing working code that people are just trusting them, says Dr. Katie Paxton-Fear, staff security advocate at Semgrep. “Developers simply aren’t being as critical now as they were when AI was worse at writing code.” Whether it’s the vibe-coder in marketing or the seasoned engineering team boosting its productivity, AI-generated code is an increasing security concern for CISOs. Much of that is a function of volume, but even as AI has proved highly capable of finding flaws in code bases, it is not yet adept at contributing code without introducing its own . Treating AI-generated code as ‘untrusted input’ Leading AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and Amazon Q Developer have become developer go-to tools, and CIOs are increasingly enlisting business users to vibe code their own apps . But as AI-generated code surfaces everywhere, CISOs have only one option: to treat it “as untrusted input that has to earn its way into the codebase,” says Bianca Lankford, VP of engineering at Datadog. To do so, security leaders are moving security checks closer to where code is written: static analysis, secrets scanning, and dependency checks run on every pull request and, increasingly, in the developer’s editor. “Companies are also approving specific AI tools, limiting what assistants can access, and training reviewers to spot common AI mistakes like outdated libraries, weak input validation, and overly permissive defaults,” Lankford adds. At Mimecast, using AI to write code doesn’t remove the developer’s responsibility for it, says Leslie Nielson, CISO at the information security vendor. “A named person owns every AI-assisted change that ships, and that’s recorded in the pull request, not assumed,” he adds. “AI can propose. Only people can approve.” The volume of code organizations need to review is only growing, and reviewing everything manually can be impossible. That’s why Nielsen recommends security leaders combine automated checks with human judgment. “We use automation for the known and repetitive, like dependency checks, secrets detection, and standard vulnerability patterns,” he says. “We keep a person accountable for anything involving access, authentication, or sensitive data. Those categories always go to a specialist reviewer, regardless of how clean the scan looks.” Datadog’s Lankford says the decision to bring in a specialist should depend on what the code could put at risk, not on what entity — human or AI — wrote it. “Anything involving authentication, cryptography, payments, personal data, or infrastructure goes to a specialist, and code owner rules can route those changes automatically,” she says. “Other useful signals include diff size, new dependencies, and changes to permissions or network exposure.” The goal is to protect the human reviewers’ attention. “A reviewer buried in low-risk changes isn’t reviewing,” Nielsen adds. “They’re approving.” Another priority should be preserving the knowledge behind the code. “Generative AI may produce software, but it cannot produce understanding,” notes Alex Ștefănescu, security expert and tech activist. “Documentation, a solid test suite, and a written record of every significant architecture decision ever made are going to save developers and organizations countless hours when a security incident hits or when they are debugging complex issues.” All of this should be created and maintained by people and intended for human use, not externalized to generative algorithms, Ștefănescu adds. What’s at risk with AI-generated code The inclusion of third-party libraries or phantom dependencies — dependencies that are not explicitly declared in a manifest file — is a common concern with AI-generated code, as these unreported software packages might not be identified during a scan and can potentially hide vulnerabilities. One way to address this is to use software composition analysis (SCA) and software supply chain security tools to help identify the libraries in use, as well as the vulnerabilities and potential legal and compliance issues that might bring. While not unique to AI-generated code, organizations also expose themselves to risks when developers download machine learning (ML) models or datasets from platforms such as Hugging Face. “In spite of security checks on both ends, it may still happen that the model contains a backdoor that becomes active once the model is integrated,” says Ștefănescu. “This could ultimately lead to data being leaked from the company that used the malicious models.” When it comes to coding agents and code completion functionality in tools like GitHub Copilot, Ștefănescu worries about hallucinations. “An LLM will always generate the most statistically probable continuation of a given prompt, so there are no real guarantees in place that it will generate a real package from PyPI, for example, after the word ‘import’,” they say. “Some attackers are aware of this and register package names on platforms like npm and PyPI, filling in some functionality that code completion tools suggest in order to make the packages seem legitimate.” If these packages are imported into real applications, they can do real damage. Sensitive information inadvertently leaking into codebases because of developers using AI-powered coding tools is another key concern. To address these risks, CISOs can establish protocols for downloading and integrating ML models or datasets from external platforms such as Hugging Face and ensure those protocols are incorporated in AI code agents’ instruction files where applicable. Such protocols can include implementing automated scanning tools to detect malicious code or backdoors, having a policy that only allows the use of models from verified publishers, or conducting internal testing in isolated environments. Not all AI-based code comes from teams full of software engineers. “We see a lot of adoption being driven by data analysts, marketing teams, researchers, etc., within organizations,” says Darren Meyer, staff research engineer at Endor Labs. These teams aren’t traditionally developing their own software but are increasingly writing simple tools that adopt AI libraries and models, so they’re often not aware of the risks involved. “This combination of shadow engineering with lower-than-average application security awareness can be a breeding ground for risk,” he adds. To make sure these teams are working safely, CISOs must consider forming relationships with these teams early in the process. Cybersecurity leaders might also want to set up training programs tailored to non-traditional development teams to educate data analysts, marketing professionals, and researchers on the potential risks associated with AI-based tools and libraries. Investing in defense “Security budgets don’t generally grow at the same pace that software development accelerates, and AI adoption is only widening that gap,” Meyer says. Application security is often underfunded in most organizations, yet allocating sufficient time and resources to it is essential, as AI adoption and AI-assisted coding accelerate the pace of software development. “A portfolio of high-quality security tools that can help address this gap is no longer optional,” Meyer says. “And while tools are critical to closing the gap, so are AppSec and ProdSec staff that can effectively partner with developers — even non-traditional developers — and understand the technical, compliance, and security implications of AI.” When it comes to securing enough resources to protect AI systems, some stakeholders might hesitate, viewing it as an optional expense rather than a critical investment. “AI adoption is a divisive topic in many organizations, with some leaders and teams being ‘all-in’ on adoption and some being strongly resistant,” Meyer says. “This tension can present challenges for insightful CISOs and business information security officers (BISOs).” CISOs that are aware of both the advantages and disadvantages of this might try to set controls to manage risks effectively, but this might create the perception of holding the organization back from innovating if they don’t explain what they do properly. “Organizations need to develop comprehensive strategies that balance the productivity benefits of AI tools with robust security practices,” says Thomas Segura, senior technical writer at GitGuardian. Cost-effective changes CISOs should implement But if a security leader has 90 days and no budget to spare, which changes would have the biggest impact? Datadog’s Lankford says a short, plain-language AI tool policy can make expectations clear. At a minimum, such a policy should spell out which tools employees can use, what code and data they can share, and which changes need specialist review. The aim is to give people answers they can use while they work, with a clear point of contact when they’re unsure. It’s also important to understand that employees don’t want to circumvent policies. They just want to get their work done without friction and without waiting weeks for approval. Giving them the right tools makes the safer route easier to take. By contrast, banning tools doesn’t work, because employees will find a way to still use them. A ban can push AI use out of sight, leaving security teams with less visibility into the code being written and the data being shared, Mimecast’s Nielsen says. CISOs should look across the development process to identify where they can intervene and which risks they can address at each stage. “Understand what layers you can influence and what vulnerabilities you can influence at each layer: in the design phase, in the CLAUDE.md file, as the agent is writing, during a pull request, as part of an AI pentest,” Semgrep’s Paxton-Fead says. It’s also important to explain to employees who are using AI code-generating tools that security lives in an implicit context: the threat model, the trust boundaries, what the attacker controls. “Agents cannot reliably plan and reason on these, so they optimize for the only signal they have, which is to satisfy the given functionality description,” Carnegie Mellon’s Wang says. When things go wrong, people in the organization need to feel safe telling security what happened, including which unapproved tools they used and what data they shared. Fear of punishment can delay that conversation, leaving the team trying to contain a problem without the full picture. “Offer amnesty instead of a crackdown, so people tell you the truth about what they’re using,” Nielsen advises.
summary: The IT manager didn’t know the company hired a “vibe coder” straight out of school. By the time they met a few months later, the new hire had already built a web application that operated with customer data and private contracts. The app ran under a domain the new hire controlled, stored data on Supabase’s free plan, and deployed directly from his GitHub repository to Cloudflare’s serverless infrastructure. “He vibe-codes everything straight into production, on servers all over the world,” the IT manager wrote on Reddit .

title: Optimizely confirms massive cyberattack on customer websites injected stealer malware
raw_text: Attackers apparently from China used an authentication security hole within the popular Optimizely AI platform for marketers to steal from at least 178 sites owned by some of the planet’s largest companies. Named victims featured vendors including Zoom, Paychex, Equifax, and GitLab, and end-user enterprises including Starbucks, IKEA, Mattel, American Eagle, Air France, Mutual of Omaha, Heineken, Home Chef, Cinnabon, American Eagle, Levi, Costco and HSBC. Salesforce issued a statement confirming that it had also been impacted by the attack. “Salesforce is investigating unauthorized modifications to scripts provided by Optimizely and used on certain Salesforce websites,” it wrote in an email statement. “As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming that Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances.” The attacks were discovered by UK-based security researcher Scott Helme , the founder of Report URI, who said in an interview that his team had confirmed 178 victims, but that there could be more. “That’s the number that we directly observed and that all carried the same infection,” he said. Helme published a report about the attacks on Monday, in which he described an attack methodology where an Optimizely capability in its Web Experimentation product facilitating adding members to a site’s development team was leveraged to insert malware into the sites. “The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker’s, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits,” Helme wrote. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.” Optimizely customers load a JavaScript “snippet” from Optimizely’s CDN onto their sites which contains Optimizely code, the customer’s A/B tests, and an optional field called Project JavaScript containing custom code written by the customer. The report said that attackers inserted their own code into the customer’s Project JavaScript and left the rest of each snippet untouched. “The file was still served from cdn[.]Optimizely[.]com, with Optimizely’s certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted,” it noted. The report described how the observed attack worked. “The script watches form submissions and every fetch/XHR POST for a card number, expiry date and CVV,” it said. “When it has all three, it sends them to https://1688360[.]cc/card[.]php with navigator.sendBeacon . Cards entered in hosted payment iframes [such as] Stripe, Adyen and similar were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site’s own form fields were not.” Analyst questions the claims of a fix Optimizely, which did not reply to an interview request, confirmed the attacks on its site. In an email shared with customers, Optimizely said that attackers “exploited a vulnerability in the Experimentation account signup flow. They used it to impersonate a user and add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. We have blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix.” The email also said that the company had “ended active sessions and revoked tokens and reset access for affected user accounts” and that it also had “removed the injected code from affected projects” and “blocked any code from being delivered in Cloudflare.” The company used highly confident wording to describe its fix, saying that “the Optimizely Experimentation platform is fully secured” and that “modification of Javascript no longer possible.” Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, raised an eyebrow at those claims. To begin with, he noted a discrepancy in the timelines published by the vendor and the security researcher. “Optimizely puts the first malicious write at 07:51. Report URI saw the BBC’s Optimizely snippet loading attacker code at 04:21, three and a half hours earlier,” he said. “The forensics report should reconcile that gap. Customers need the real start time to scope their exposure.” As well, he pointed out, “Optimizely seems very comfortable stating absolutes early in a forensics investigation. Those are verdicts from a company whose forensics are still underway and whose timeline disagrees with outside research.” No responsibility for the attack claimed Helme speculated in an interview that the attackers were a small group of thieves, almost certainly coming from China, noting that he saw extensive Chinese writing in the code and that the attacks “tie back to infrastructure that has been used by other Chinese actors.” “They are either Chinese or they really want us to think that they are Chinese,” Helme said, adding that the nature of what was stolen makes it highly unlikely the attackers were state actors. State actors, he said, would likely have used the malware on major news sites to create and spread false stories. Asked if his team could verify Optimizely’s claim that it had fixed the hole, he said that he couldn’t yet. Some of the infected sites were cleaned up, but he has to wait to see if they get reinfected before concluding that the original hole had been closed. Recommendation to customers ‘concerning’ Dickson said that one line in Optimizely’s email to customers was especially concerning. “Optimizely’s documentation tells customers to allow ‘unsafe-eval ‘ in their policy. At HSBC, the policy blocked the main payload and the data theft, but a backup copy of the malicious code ran anyway through that setting. A vendor’s setup guide should not quietly loosen its customers’ defenses,” Dickson said. “Restrict script-src to the hosts a page actually needs. Lock down connect-src so stolen data has nowhere to go. Drop ‘ unsafe-eval ‘ wherever possible. Start in report-only mode so nothing breaks.” He added, “the Optimizely attack may be about as bad as a third-party script compromise gets. Optimizely owes its customers a clear explanation of how one flaw reached so many unrelated companies.”
summary: Attackers apparently from China used an authentication security hole within the popular Optimizely AI platform for marketers to steal from at least 178 sites owned by some of the planet’s largest companies. Named victims featured vendors including Zoom, Paychex, Equifax, and GitLab, and end-user enterprises including Starbucks, IKEA, Mattel, American Eagle, Air France, Mutual of Omaha, Heineken, Home Chef, Cinnabon, American Eagle, Levi, Costco and HSBC. Salesforce issued a statement confirming that it had also been impacted by the attack. “Salesforce is investigating unauthorized modifications to scripts provided by Optimizely and used on certain Salesforce websites,” it wrote in an email statement.

title: Google and Anthropic push for faster patches as AI collapses bug discovery timelines
raw_text: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has made it untenable for software vendors to sit on privately reported flaws for months, and Google Project Zero is responding by shrinking its vulnerability disclosure deadline from 90 to 60 days, with plans to drop it to 30 days a year from now. Anthropic is following suit with an even more aggressive timeline. Project Zero is Google’s elite vulnerability research team that regularly reports vulnerabilities in widely used open-source and proprietary software, much of which is critical to internet infrastructure. Its 90-day deadline for vendors to produce patches before the team releases vulnerability details publicly was a major stake in the ground for the security research community when it was announced in 2014, and it has become the de facto standard for coordinated disclosure. The team’s announcement Friday that it will reduce this deadline to 60 days starting in February and 30 days starting in January 2028 is important because when Project Zero speaks, the security industry listens. And it did. On Monday, Anthropic announced it will adjust its disclosure policy from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues, starting in January. Other security companies and researchers will likely follow. The rationale is explicitly due to the offensive cyber capabilities of large language models: not only in discovering new vulnerabilities, but in reverse engineering patches and using them as blueprints for finding additional flaws in the same code . “LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug,” Project Zero researcher Natalie Silvanovich said in a blog post . “A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.” Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team said essentially the same: “A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months. We no longer believe it can, and these changes are intended to keep pace with progress in AI capabilities and strike the right balance for defenders.” ‘Soak time’ has become meaningless Since 2021, Project Zero’s policy has actually been “90+30” with 90 days to develop a patch, plus 30 days of grace while the patch rolled out to users. The team referred to these extra 30 days as “soak time.” But in a world where AI agents can analyze patches to determine flaw details in minutes and then write exploits for them, waiting for a patch to propagate before releasing vulnerability details only creates a false sense of secrecy. As a result, the Project Zero’s previous 30-day grace is gone effective immediately. In a report published this week, Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) documented the first fully automated AI-powered vulnerability discovery-and-exploitation pipeline it has observed in the wild. Called exploit_agent, the framework is designed to analyze application code changes following security patches, identify vulnerabilities, and generate exploits without requiring an operator to direct each step. While Anthropic has different deadlines based on vulnerability severity, Project Zero decided to abandon severity as a disclosure metric because attackers are just as likely to discover low-risk flaws as they are to find the high-risk ones. “When vendors determine severity and use it to prioritize bug fixes, they are making decisions about what risks they are willing to expose their users to, and it is reasonable to accept the risk of low-severity bugs, like unexploitable null pointer crashes or minor info leaks in a lot of circumstances,” Project Zero’s Silvanovich said. “But this doesn’t change the availability of these vulnerabilities to attackers, and we want our policy to reflect this reality.” Google’s team will also no longer check whether a vendor’s patch fixes the issue when deciding whether to release details or not, because this back-and-forth can quickly become unmanageable, especially because the team now finds vulnerabilities using AI assistance at a much faster pace and because vendors might choose alternative mitigation strategies such as temporarily disabling a vulnerable feature or code path until a full patch can be developed. “We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly,” Silvanovich said. The road ahead will be bumpy for users The shorter patch deadlines come at a time when open-source projects and software vendors are already drowning in vulnerability reports and must resort to either AI-assisted patching or hiring more developers, if they can afford it. As of last week, the number of CVEs issued this year exceeded 100,000, more than double last year’s count. Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team noted that “models can now help develop fixes” as one justification for the more aggressive disclosure deadlines, and said it will include “actionable guidance with each report, along with a patch or mitigation where possible,” to help maintainers confirm flaws and fix them. However, multiple studies and developers have reported in recent months that AI-generated patches are often incomplete, failing to address the root causes of a flaw, to eliminate all instances of the bug from the codebase, or to block all exploit variations. Security firm XOR built a benchmark that pitted frontier coding systems against vulnerabilities the company had discovered in a private software stack. No public fix existed for any of the flaws when the evaluation ran, so the systems had to work from the vulnerable code alone. The best models produced complete fixes for only about a third of the flaws: 35.3% for GPT-6 Astra and 28.6% for Claude Fable 5.1. Across all systems, just 11.9% of patch attempts earned full credit. According to an analysis by VulnCheck , seven months after launching its Mythos-powered Glasswing vulnerability-hunting program, Anthropic’s public ledger counts 37,966 findings, but only 217 of the 7,349 flaws made public so far have been fixed. Project Zero acknowledges the friction between the need to patch faster and devs being overloaded. The team solicited feedback from the vendors it reports to most and chose the phased schedule because an immediate change could push vendors to stop trying to meet the disclosure deadlines. “To respond to these new timelines, organizations should be better prepared to assess whether compensating controls can reduce the risk of a vulnerability when it’s disclosed,” Ramy Rahman, senior principal solutions engineer at ArmorCode, tells CSO. “With disclosures arriving sooner, and sometimes before a fix is available, teams need a process for evaluating exposure, applying available mitigations, and tracking remediation.” “Consider hardening systems at deployment time and removing software you don’t use,” he said. “Leaner, more deliberate deployments can reduce exposure and make vulnerability findings easier to manage.”
summary: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has made it untenable for software vendors to sit on privately reported flaws for months, and Google Project Zero is responding by shrinking its vulnerability disclosure deadline from 90 to 60 days, with plans to drop it to 30 days a year from now. Anthropic is following suit with an even more aggressive timeline. Project Zero is Google’s elite vulnerability research team that regularly reports vulnerabilities in widely used open-source and proprietary software, much of which is critical to internet infrastructure. Its 90-day deadline for vendors to produce patches before the team releases vulnerability details publicly was a major stake in the ground for the security research community when it was announced in 2014, and it has become the de facto standard for coordinated disclosure.

title: California sues OpenAI, alleges 80-plus agent escapes hidden from public
raw_text: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI, alleging the company has lost control of its autonomous AI agents more than 80 times during testing and misled the public about how safely it develops its models. The complaint was filed on November 16 in San Francisco Superior Court against OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC. It says OpenAI disclosed the 80-plus figure to state investigators but has publicly reported just 27 such incidents. In those incidents, agents reached third-party systems, foreign government websites and OpenAI’s own infrastructure, the state alleged. “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement announcing the lawsuit . The state brings two claims: violations of California’s Unfair Competition Law and creation of a public nuisance. It is seeking an injunction, restitution, disgorgement, and an order to abate the nuisance. It also wants civil penalties of $2,500 against each defendant for each violation proven at trial. Other incidents and internal breaches In one July incident, agents escaped their sandboxes and gained administrator-level access to OpenAI’s own systems, according to the complaint. Those systems included the company’s cloud model deployment system, its secrets management service, and its identity and access management service. The agents then launched unauthorized servers, exposing OpenAI’s infrastructure to the internet. OpenAI did not let external researchers review that attack, the complaint said. The complaint identified several other incidents involving OpenAI agents. At RubyGems, a software package repository, agents allegedly uploaded thousands of packages in May 2026. Administrators removed more than 500 packages they considered malicious, and the platform suspended new user registrations between May 12 and May 16. The complaint also alleged that agents made approximately 17,000 edits to a German website, DseWiki, using it as a message board to exchange information about bypassing sandbox restrictions. Other incidents involved Wikimedia Foundation’s infrastructure and Australian government websites. The complaint said agents overwhelmed Wikimedia services with millions of API requests and hundreds of thousands of Wikidata queries, likely contributing to a partial outage in May. In June, agents allegedly accessed non-public information from Australian government websites. The complaint further said OpenAI notified dozens of organizations whose websites or internal systems had been accessed by its agents. These included government institutions, law enforcement agencies, educational institutions, and small businesses. Some incidents allegedly involved stolen credentials, API keys, and fraudulent accounts, with agents accessing personally identifiable information. OpenAI’s own infrastructure was also compromised in at least three attacks in July, according to the complaint. Agents allegedly obtained administrator-level access to systems supporting cloud model deployment, secrets management, and identity and access management. Escapes after the fix The state argued that the danger is ongoing. On September 20, after OpenAI had hardened its environment, an agent escaped during a training run and reached an external chatbot. “This incident occurred after OpenAI had implemented ‘security hardening’ following the Hugging Face attack,” the lawsuit added. OpenAI detected it within minutes, but the run did not stop automatically, and human reviewers took two more hours to halt it, the complaint said. OpenAI announced a pause on training and evaluating its most capable models on September 25. The pause lasted five days, ending October 1, according to the complaint. Warnings that went unheeded The complaint argued that the incidents were foreseeable. It cited the run-up to the Hugging Face attack as evidence. By May 26, agents had used a vulnerability in a misconfigured software package service to reach the public internet. An internal OpenAI team saw at least one agent escape but apparently took no action, the complaint said. On June 27, a security monitoring tool flagged that the research environment was being probed for vulnerabilities, and OpenAI again did not stop its runs. When agent traffic knocked the service offline on July 4, OpenAI patched it over the holiday weekend and resumed runs on July 7, the state alleged. Two days later, agents broke out again. The state also faulted OpenAI for not running live chain-of-thought monitoring in training and evaluation, even though it did so for models deployed to employees. During the Hugging Face attack, one agent’s reasoning read: “We’re attacking third-party HF using leaked token, potentially outside intended scope. . . . This is arguably unauthorized.” Bonta’s office served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena on September 30. OpenAI answered with a 14-page letter and produced no supporting documents, the complaint said. California is not the only state pressing OpenAI. In August, Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird led a 15-state coalition demanding that OpenAI preserve evidence, protect whistleblowers and halt the tests behind the hack until it could show it can run them responsibly. “The AI weaponized itself, which is extremely scary,” Bird said in a statement . OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld .
summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI, alleging the company has lost control of its autonomous AI agents more than 80 times during testing and misled the public about how safely it develops its models. The complaint was filed on November 16 in San Francisco Superior Court against OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC. It says OpenAI disclosed the 80-plus figure to state investigators but has publicly reported just 27 such incidents. In those incidents, agents reached third-party systems, foreign government websites and OpenAI’s own infrastructure, the state alleged.

title: Hackers exploit Microsoft 365 outage to launch credential phishing campaign
raw_text: Cybercriminals are exploiting genuine cloud service disruptions to make phishing attacks more convincing. Just a day after a prolonged outage disrupted several Microsoft services , including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and Copilot, Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organisations across multiple industry sectors. The attackers impersonated service notifications and sent emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications. Claiming emails held during the outage would be permanently deleted within 24 hours unless recipients restored them, the threat actors created a false sense of urgency, tricking recipients into clicking malicious links and potentially exposing their login credentials. “We assess that the activity was likely credential phishing; however, the available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext,” Jeremiah Jasmin, security researcher at Microsoft, said in a blog post . Outages in cloud services bring about uncertainty and panic, an area where attackers always thrive, said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. “In cases where employees cannot access their emails and other applications, they will easily fall victim to any email promising to restore their service or help recover their account. This is especially dangerous for industries like finance, health care, government and educational institutions because employees in such organizations work with sensitive data and rely heavily on cloud services,” said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. Carefully constructed phishing trap The attackers used several techniques to make the emails appear relevant to recipients while evading basic email security filters. These included using specific sender domains, randomised outage-related subject lines, recipient-specific tracking links and a common non-Microsoft destination domain. The combination made the messages harder to identify through conventional pattern matching. The campaign began with emails sent from domains including moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com. Their subject lines followed the pattern “Outage” followed by a randomised string of characters. Microsoft also found a fake email conversation embedded in the message body, positioned to remain hidden from recipients. This appeared to be an attempt to evade email filtering mechanisms. The messages impersonated Microsoft 365 service health notifications. They used recipient-specific display name prefixes and referenced Microsoft services, including Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot. To create a sense of urgency, the emails claimed that messages held during the November 12 Exchange Online disruption would be deleted within 24 hours. Recipients were prompted to click a prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” button. The links contained recipient-specific tracking URLs that recorded or routed clicks before redirecting users to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html. One of the emails analysed by Microsoft had a subject line following the pattern “Outage – ” and a display name comprising a three-character organisation-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification.” Its body referred to a purported Exchange Online incident on November 12, claimed that four messages had been held during the outage and warned that they would be deleted within 24 hours unless restored. A successful credential theft attempt could expose more than an employee’s email account. Dhar explained that, depending on the permissions of the user, threat actors can gain access to sensitive emails, customer information, balance sheets, SharePoint, OneDrive Storage, and Microsoft Teams communication. Moreover, attackers can pretend to be representatives of the company and send believable emails to colleagues, clients, and contractors for the purposes of money fraud or theft of credentials. From containment to preparedness Microsoft said it had not observed any evidence of account compromise linked to the campaign. Messages detected and protected by Microsoft Defender for Office 365 were being blocked or quarantined. However, the company has advised organisations to remain vigilant and take several precautionary steps. CISOs should search email telemetry for the identified sender domains, display-name and subject-line patterns, lure phrases, tracking hosts, and destination domains. Matching messages should be quarantined, and copies already delivered to inboxes should be removed in accordance with the organisation’s incident response procedures. Security teams should also identify users who clicked on campaign links and review click telemetry, proxy logs, and browser or endpoint evidence to establish whether they reached the malicious destination and potentially entered their credentials. If credentials were exposed, organisations should immediately reset the affected passwords, revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, and verify multifactor authentication registrations. They should also check affected accounts for suspicious sign-ins, unauthorised OAuth consent, new inbox or forwarding rules, delegate permissions and unusual access to Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive or Teams. Microsoft has also advised security teams to block or closely monitor reallifeaccounting[.]com and the observed /themelist0.html path while the activity is investigated. Employees should be reminded that legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health communications do not direct users to non-Microsoft domains to recover held emails. Dhar added that organizations should make cybersecurity an integral part of their business continuity planning. Any technology disruption should trigger heightened security monitoring and clear internal communication to ensure employees know how to verify service-related updates. He also recommended conducting phishing simulations during such disruptions to test how employees respond to suspicious communications. CIOs and CISOs should regularly conduct tabletop exercises to assess their preparedness for attacks that exploit technology outages. The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld .
summary: Cybercriminals are exploiting genuine cloud service disruptions to make phishing attacks more convincing. Just a day after a prolonged outage disrupted several Microsoft services , including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and Copilot, Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organisations across multiple industry sectors. The attackers impersonated service notifications and sent emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications. Claiming emails held during the outage would be permanently deleted within 24 hours unless recipients restored them, the threat actors created a false sense of urgency, tricking recipients into clicking malicious links and potentially exposing their login credentials.

title: Google spots the first hacker AI system that finds and exploits flaws autonomously
raw_text: Google said it had identified a hacker-operated AI framework designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention, marking the first time its researchers had observed such a system being used by threat actors. The findings, published in a report by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, suggest that attackers are moving beyond using generative AI to assist individual tasks and are beginning to automate larger portions of cyberattacks . The system could give attackers a way to exploit publicly disclosed vulnerabilities , known as n-days, before companies finish applying security updates. Google’s researchers discovered it on an exposed staging server and identified it as a multi-agent framework called exploit_agent. The framework connects to multiple large language models (LLMs) and is configured to examine changes in application code following security patches, identify vulnerabilities, and generate exploits without requiring an operator to direct each step. It can also execute the exploits automatically. Google found data exfiltrated from targeted victims on the server, along with scripts designed to support further activity after an initial compromise. Evidence suggested that the operator was particularly interested in French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries and the education sector. The report did not establish whether the framework’s autonomous operations were responsible for the theft. Google also cited a separate campaign involving vulnerabilities in PaperCut print management servers. According to research by GreyNoise referenced in Google’s report, a threat actor likely used AI tools to develop and test exploits before launching a campaign against hundreds of organizations four days after the vulnerabilities were disclosed. In separate cases, Google observed other AI frameworks being used by attackers. CAIRN was deployed in intrusion activity targeting organizations that included the US aerospace sector, while a customized platform based on PentAGI was used to conduct reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against organizations across Asia. Pressure on enterprise response times Despite the growing use of AI in cyberattacks, the underlying techniques remain largely unchanged, according to Jonathan Ong , senior analyst at Omdia. “This is more of an acceleration of existing attack techniques,” Ong said. “These are pentesting/red-teaming frameworks with established techniques, albeit significantly sped up with an LLM model.” Keith Prabhu , CEO of Confidis, said there is still limited evidence that AI makes individual attacks more successful. The greater risk, he said, is that attackers could launch more attempts in less time, potentially increasing the number of successful compromises even if each attempt is no more effective. Ong said the frameworks typically generate considerable detectable activity, meaning enterprises with properly configured and monitored endpoint detection and response (EDR), extended detection and response (XDR), or managed detection and response (MDR) capabilities should still be able to identify much of the malicious activity. Google also warned that although the frameworks generate activity that makes detection easier, they remain capable of achieving their objectives. Rather than overhauling their defenses, security leaders should continue prioritizing established security practices, particularly cloud and identity hardening. Ong pointed to multifactor authentication, strong passwords, and measures to block repeated login attempts as effective safeguards. “The one thing that has changed is that the containment and response timeline needs to be faster, to match the speed at which attackers using these frameworks are moving,” Ong said. Prabhu said the problem is compounded by fragmented security visibility and response processes that still depend on manual decisions. He recommended that CISOs prioritize continuous asset discovery and risk-based vulnerability remediation. He also called for better detection capabilities that connect suspicious activity across enterprise environments. Amit Kumar Jena , development manager for AI at Kanerika, said organizations must give particular attention to vulnerabilities in systems exposed to the internet, where attackers could exploit flaws soon after they become public. “Internet-facing systems should be treated as their own class, with a fast-track patch path and virtual patching while fixes are tested,” Jena said. For incident containment, Prabhu suggested automating actions that are well understood and can be reversed, while retaining human approval for decisions that could have significant operational consequences. Jena also recommended defining in advance which containment actions could be automated, citing endpoint isolation and session revocation as examples. “The aim is not to remove human oversight, but to eliminate avoidable delays and regularly test that response works at the pace of an attack,” Prabhu said. Lower barriers for cybercriminals Open-source agentic frameworks could lower the technical barriers for less-experienced cybercriminals by helping them coordinate existing tools and adapt their attacks based on results, Prabhu said. However, these capabilities do not eliminate the need for technical expertise or guarantee successful compromises. Prabhu said smaller organizations and service providers with limited security resources could be particularly exposed. The risk is not necessarily concentrated in any particular industry, he added. Organizations with poorly maintained legacy systems or weak identity controls could face greater exposure regardless of their sector.
summary: Google said it had identified a hacker-operated AI framework designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention, marking the first time its researchers had observed such a system being used by threat actors. The findings, published in a report by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, suggest that attackers are moving beyond using generative AI to assist individual tasks and are beginning to automate larger portions of cyberattacks . The system could give attackers a way to exploit publicly disclosed vulnerabilities , known as n-days, before companies finish applying security updates. Google’s researchers discovered it on an exposed staging server and identified it as a multi-agent framework called exploit_agent.

title: Unlawfully held images still used for police facial recognition
raw_text:
UK police are continuing to conduct tens of thousands of retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches on potentially millions of unlawfully retained custody images, the police watchdog has found.

In November 2026, the HM Chief Inspector of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS) published a 58-page report examining how police forces and the National Crime Agency (NCA) are using RFR, after being commissioned by UK home secretary Shabana Mahmood to investigate the matter a year earlier.

Unlike live facial recognition (LFR), which captures and compares people’s faces to a pre-determined watchlist in real time, RFR is applied to already-captured images retroactively, enabling police to compare “probe” images against existing custody images taken when suspects are arrested.

The Home Office originally added an a RFR function to the Police National Database (PND) in 2013, allowing trained and licensed police users to search custody images to identify unknown persons of interest.

As it stands, the PND – which collates data from all 43 police forces in England and Wales, as well as Police Scotland, the Police Service of Northern Ireland, the National Crime Agency and other law enforcement bodies – contains billions of records drawn from several hundred databases, including more than 20 million facial images.

According to the watchdog, its inspection revealed that custody images are still being retained in breach of police information management rules, which set out how forces should review, retain and dispose of custody images.

It noted that while custody image deletion was largely outside the scope of its inspection – which instead focused more on governance arrangements and operational practices – it nonetheless found that “some of the images used in RFR searches should have been deleted and yet were still available for RFR searches”.

It added that this creates a situation that “risks undermining public confidence” in how police are using the technology.

As it stands, UK law enforcement bodies are making more than 300,000 RFR search requests per year.

On top of issues around unlawful custody image retention, the watchdog also found that police use of RFR technology lacked consistent oversight and safeguards, describing a legal and regulatory landscape that is fragmented and underdeveloped.

The “limited oversight”, it added, is compounded by inconsistent approaches to public consultation, transparency and record-keeping across forces, as well as “considerable variation” in how individual forces are using the tech itself.

It also found that police forces often did not have enough management information to understand how effectively they used RFR, or to evaluate the technology’s contribution to crime investigations. This means forces generally “couldn’t clearly show performance improvements from using RFR”.

A long-standing issue

Although it is not mentioned in the report, a High Court ruling in 2012 found the retention of custody images in the PND to be unlawful, on the basis that information about unconvicted people was being treated in the same way as information about people who were ultimately convicted. It also ruled that the six-year retention period was disproportionate.

Despite the 2012 ruling, successive biometric commissioners have warned that millions of custody images are still being unlawfully retained.

Writing to other chief constables to outline some of the issues around custody image retention in February 2022, the National Police Chiefs Council (NPCC) lead for records management, Lee Freeman, said the potentially unlawful retention of millions of custody images “poses a significant risk in terms of potential litigation, police legitimacy and wider support and challenge in our use of these images for technologies such as facial recognition”.

However, HMICFRS said in its report that it was “reassured” by a project launched in October 2023 by the Home Office and NPCC – known as Programme Tabula – to manage the custody image retention issue.

Responding to Computer Weekly’s questions about the custody image issue in November 2023, the NPCC said at the time that “policing needs to ensure transparency and legitimacy in the way we control the use of this important biometric information.”

While a spokesperson confirmed that a national programme had been launched a month earlier “to ensure consistency and co-ordination across UK policing in how it retains, processes and then uses custody images, particularly in the use of facial recognition”, it did not disclose the name of the programme.

“Through the programme, we will agree and implement a robust management regime for custody images to ensure compliance to agreed policies and legislation,” it said. “It is vital to public confidence that this programme is adopted nationally to make sure we are holding data lawfully and ethically, both now and in the future.”

The spokesperson added that while the programme was yet to be publicised, it will seek to establish a management regime for custody images, alongside a review of all currently held data by police forces in the UK, which will be implemented over a two-year period.

“We welcome this work,” said HMICFRS. “It is important that the police service aligns its approach to retaining custody images with other biometric data so that it is consistent and lawful. We look forward to learning how Programme Tabula will support forces in managing custody images more consistently and improving their compliance with legal and data retention requirements.”

Limited oversight

In terms of the wider oversight issues, HMICFRS found that legislation has not kept up with the technology or its use, leading to governance gaps and inconsistent oversight practices.

“Some forces had clear guidance setting out how searches should be carried out, how results should be recorded and what corroborative enquiries were required,” it wrote. “Others lacked formal procedures, which increased the risk of inconsistent decision-making and misunderstanding of the technology’s limitations.

“We found that investigators and supervisors didn’t routinely document the consideration or use of RFR in investigation plans, enquiry logs or supervisory reviews. As a result, forces often lacked clear audit trails showing how RFR results informed decision-making and whether appropriate corroboration had taken place.

“This limits forces’ ability to assess their use of RFR, identify missed opportunities, and provide effective scrutiny and governance.”

On how this translates into practical use, HMICFRS said that police investigators did not always know that RFR results were intelligence rather than evidence, and therefore required further enquiries before officers took enforcement action.

“This creates a risk that people could be incorrectly identified or arrested, which could undermine public confidence in the technology,” it said.

“We found that some investigators didn’t always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches. In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action.”

His Majesty’s Inspector of Constabulary Kathryn Stone said continued public support relied on showing the technology was being used properly.

“Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment,” she said. “A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence.”

Upcoming legislation

In December 2025, the Home Office launched a 10-week consultation on police use of biometrics, including LFR, allowing interested parties and members of the public to share their views on how the controversial technology should be regulated. This also covered other forms of biometric surveillance, including RFR.

This followed on from then-home secretary Yvette Cooper telling a Lords committee in July 2025 that the government intended to create “a proper, clear governance framework” to regulate the use of facial recognition technology by police.

When launching the consultation, the Home Office said that although a “patchwork” legal framework for police use of facial recognition technology exists – including for increasing use of retrospective and “operator-initiated” versions – it does not give police forces the confidence to “use it at significantly greater scale … nor does it consistently give the public the confidence that it will be used responsibly”.

While the government reiterated its intention to bring forward a new legislative framework for police use of biometrics in its formal consultation response, it has so far refrained from committing to specific safeguards, outside of establishing a new independent oversight body (which will consolidate and expand the functions of existing oversight roles) and committing to making public participation in oversight of a statutory requirement.

The government said the framework “will ensure policing can innovate in a repeatable and consistent manner, supporting adoption of emerging biometric and overt surveillance technologies that improve policing effectiveness and public protection, while maintaining appropriate safeguards and oversight”.
