title: Google widens sovereign cloud with Gemini, key and audit tools
raw_text:
Google has added Gemini models to Google Cloud Dedicated, its partner-operated sovereign cloud offering, to widen the choice of artificial intelligence (AI) available to organisations that need locally controlled infrastructure.

The company announced the change at its Sovereign AI Summit in Brussels this week, alongside a preview of confidential external key management (cEKM) and new audit frameworks that map regulation to enforced controls.

Sovereign cloud offerings from Google come in three forms:

  1. Google Cloud Data Boundary, which applies data residency, access and encryption controls on the public cloud;
  2. Google Cloud Dedicated, which is isolated infrastructure operated by an independent local partner;
  3. Google Distributed Cloud, which runs in a customer’s own datacentre, and can be connected or fully air-gapped.

Google introduced the three-tier portfolio in May 2025 and set out its underlying commitments in February 2026 to cover local investment, operational continuity, customer control of data and open technology. The Brussels announcements build on that base rather than replacing it.

Gemini already runs in Google Cloud under a commitment to process customer data in-region, and on Google Distributed Cloud. In France, S3NS has made managed model serving and inference generally available on PREMI3NS, its cloud built on Google Cloud Dedicated. Teams can deploy open models from Mistral and Google, or their own tuned models, inside an environment S3NS controls.

Confidential external key management, now in preview, lets customers or local partners hold root keys outside Google Cloud while key operations run inside a hardware-attested Confidential Computing environment. Google said the design keeps latency low and reliability high. A partnership with Telefónica, also in preview, adds Spain to the countries where organisations can hold keys locally, alongside France, Germany and Italy. Key custody is a common sticking point in regulated procurement, where buyers must show who controls encryption.

S3NS and the Thales German launch

Google’s European sovereign cloud rests on local operators. In France, S3NS – the Thales and Google Cloud joint venture – has achieved SecNumCloud 3.2 qualification from ANSSI, the national cyber security agency, and now serves more than 130 customers. Thales is moving 80% of its own applications onto the platform.

Hélène Bringer, president of S3NS, said the venture’s proposition was “to have data sovereignty in our trusted cloud”. S3NS struck a flagship partnership with SAP in May, with SAP Rise set to become the second software-as-a-service (SaaS) solution on PREMI3NS next year.

The model is now moving into Germany. With Thales, Google Cloud Dedicated is in preview there, run from three datacentres in Berlin. Marcus Mühling, chief executive of Secure Cloud Germany, said the local operation had submitted its C3A documentation to the BSI, Germany’s federal cyber security agency, on 1 October and received positive feedback. It is working towards ISO 27001 and C5 certification by the end of the first quarter, with operations due in the second quarter.

“If your clients have to make extreme choices – either sovereignty or innovation – that’s broken,” Mühling said.

Meanwhile, Data Boundary frameworks aim to map local and regional regulatory requirements to enforced, auditable controls. A framework for Switzerland is available now, and Google plans one for the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act (Dora) for financial services next. Audit Manager then gives auditors continuous, machine-readable evidence. Google positioned the frameworks as a way to cut the engineering effort that sovereignty audits usually demand, which can be a persistent drag on regulated cloud projects.

Regulated workloads often stall because the security, identity and monitoring tools teams rely on are missing from a sovereign environment. Google said more than a dozen software suppliers, including European providers Memority and Tsuga, have now validated their products on Google Cloud Dedicated to close that gap.

It also launched the Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI, an equity-free programme that gives startups in regulated sectors engineering support, mentorship and access to local cloud providers.

Marianne Janik, vice-president for EMEA North at Google Cloud, said the release removed a long-standing trade-off. “Organisations that need a locally operated cloud will no longer have to choose between frontier AI and control,” she said. “Alongside Gemini, we’re announcing four more ways to put control in your hands.”

Google frames sovereignty as a property of the whole stack. Janik argued that a stack is only as sovereign as its weakest layer – the layer a customer cannot control or replace – and that the answer is a composable stack with verifiable controls and exit options at every layer.

Google has pitched the portfolio on verifiable control. That answers critics who argue that hyperscaler sovereignty commitments rest on trust.

Its Cloud Dedicated offer lets customers block software updates in exceptional circumstances and keep operating for up to 12 months if their connection to Google is severed. This aims to answer the continuity concern that underpins the “kill switch” debate.

Google’s sovereign cloud push matters beyond the EU. UK organisations that run workloads in Europe face the same questions, and UK CIOs are watching how far the EU’s Cloud and AI Development Act (Cada) reaches as Brussels builds out its full-stack sovereignty package.

The practical test will be evidence of deployments. Buyers increasingly have to show regulators and auditors how data and keys are held, who can access them and what happens if a provider is cut off.

title: Fintech pioneer Anne Boden back with agentic AI-focused bank
raw_text:
Starling bank founder Anne Boden has revealed her next venture to be an agentic artificial intelligence (AI)-focused bank.

The bank, Lockwood, will initially attempt to gain an Electronic Money Institution (EMI) licence from the Financial Conduct Authority in 2027, before a full banking licence in 2028. It is targeting one million customers in its first year.

Boden, who left Starling in 2023, sold her shares in the firm, and is reported to be providing the new company’s initial funding.

She told The Sunday Times that the bank is “going to be built by agents, to serve customers that want to use agents, and then be defended by agents”.

On its website, Lockwood describes its approach to AI and its security. “You’re ready to welcome AI assistants into your life, with all the convenience and financial freedom they offer,” it says. “Yet, at the same time, more fraudsters are using AI to try to break into people’s accounts. Most banks will respond with more passwords, more checks and more tracking. Lockwood is different. Lockwood is building its current account with fewer ways in, and Lockwood guards every one of them.”

According to Lockwood, it is a current account that “lets your AI agent pay for things safely, within limits you set, for people and small businesses in the UK.”

“Ten years ago, we built digital banking around the smartphone,” she said. “Today, the interface of personal finance is shifting again – from apps that you tap to intelligent agents that act on your behalf. If an AI agent is going to shop for you, pay your bills or manage your money, your bank account needs to be engineered specifically to govern that relationship safely. Lockwood is about giving people the confidence to embrace agentic AI while keeping absolute control over their finances.”

Boden founded Starling in 2014, and it received its banking licence in 2016, launching the following year. In October 2020, it made its first monthly profit of £800,000, becoming the first UK digital challenger bank to do so, and it reached fintech unicorn status in 2021.

Read more about Boden: Banker’s startup experience feathers the nest for Starling Bank

Boden is an IT professional who got into banking. She gained a BSc in computer science and chemistry, and an MBA.

Boden joined Lloyds Bank in the early 1980s, when, as she told Computer Weekly in a 2015 interview, she was “doing fintech before fintech was fashionable”.

After Lloyds Bank, her career has included a period heading up UK IT at Standard Chartered; being one of the original designers of the Clearing House Automated Payments System; a role as a strategy and technology consultant at PWC; restructuring European operations at UBS; holding the global chief information officer job for reinsurance at Aon; and running business in 34 countries for ABN Amro, and subsequently RBS, when it took over the Dutch bank.

But it was after leaving RBS in 2011 – to spend time working with startups to find out what was going on in financial services outside the big organisations – that she realised how banks needed to change. She joined Allied Irish Bank as chief operating officer and began implementing some of the ideas she’d had while working with small fintech groups. This was successful for the bank, but Boden wanted more – and realised the only way to get it was by starting from scratch with a new bank when the time was right.

title: The big cyber short, or dot AI bubble?
raw_text:
The AI build-out will not cause a repeat of the 2008 financial crisis. It is far more likely to cause a repeat of 2000, and that is not the reassurance it sounds like. A dotcom-style bust would still wipe trillions from markets, take a decade or more to recover, and arrive at a moment when the world has less slack to absorb it than it had in either 2000 or 2008.

I watched The Big Short again this week. What struck me was not the collapse. It was the 18 months before it, when a handful of investors read the loan tapes, saw that the collateral could not support the paper, and bought insurance against it while the sellers kept selling.

Boards ask me a simple question. Could the AI bubble produce a crisis on the scale of the subprime collapse, one that freezes credit, takes down counterparties and reaches every balance sheet on the planet? My answer has three parts. A sharp correction is now more likely than not within two to three years. The shape of that correction will look more like the dot-com bust than Lehman. And a full 2008-scale systemic event is a minority outcome, perhaps one chance in five. One in five is not a tail risk. It is a planning assumption.

The reasons the systemic probability is lower than 2008 are structural. So are the reasons the correction probability is high. Both deserve a plain explanation, because the damage will not land where most executives think it will.

2008 vs. 2000

Subprime was not a housing problem. It was a leverage and disclosure problem that used housing as raw material. Mortgages became bonds, bonds became collateralised debt obligations (CDOs), which became synthetic CDOs referencing other CDOs. The paper outstanding was a multiple of the loans beneath it, and the demand for it was partly manufactured. Goldman Sachs sold more than $40bn of mortgage securities in 2006 and 2007 while its own desk, on the chief financial officer’s instruction, shorted the market. It did not tell the buyers – pension funds, insurers, unions and foreign banks.

Three features made it systemic. The banks that ran the payment system were the holders, levered 30 to one. The instruments were opaque, so nobody could price a counterparty. And the collateral was a single asset class that fell everywhere at once. Remove any one of those and 2008 becomes a bad year rather than a near-death experience for the global financial system.

However, the dotcom bust was a valuation collapse, not a credit collapse, and that distinction is the whole argument. The Nasdaq peaked at 5,048 on 10 March 2000 and fell 78 per cent to 1,114 by October 2002, erasing roughly five trillion dollars of market value. It did not regain its high until April 2015.

The companies that died deserved to. Only about 14% of Nasdaq-100 IPOs were profitable at the top. Pets.com booked $5.8m of revenue against a $61.8m loss and was delisted within a year. Cisco, the picks-and-shovels supplier to the internet, traded at 201 times earnings and 20 times sales.

Yet the banks held. The payment system never froze. The US economy had a short, shallow recession, and the technology turned out to be everything its promoters claimed. The losses fell on equity holders, on employees paid in options, and on the pension funds that had drifted into growth stocks. That is a very different casualty list from 2008, and it is why most investors today reach for 2000 as the comforting precedent.

The AI build-out by the numbers

AI stopped being an equity story in 2025 and became a debt story. American AI companies raised $217bn of debt last year, had passed $445bn by mid-August 2026, and are expected by Morgan Stanley to reach close to $600bn for the year. Hyperscaler leverage doubled from 0.9 to 1.8 times in roughly six months.

The cash that used to pay for this has turned. Google’s free cash flow went negative in the second quarter of 2026 for the first time since its listing. The paper that does not appear on any balance sheet has grown: Goldman counts $1.5tn of lease commitments, a trillion of which have not started, and another $1.5tn of purchase commitments for chips and power.

The second tier is where 2000 and 2008 meet. Neocloud providers such as CoreWeave carry debt approaching $50bn, mostly floating-rate private credit from Blackstone, Apollo, BlackRock and Magnetar. The collateral is GPUs with a three-to-five-year life. CoreWeave’s five-year credit default swap touched 1,195 basis points on 15 October, pricing a default probability above sixty per cent.

And the revenue to carry all of it is not there yet. Bain estimates the industry needs $2tn of annual revenue by 2030 to pay for its compute and will fall about $800bn short. MIT research found 95% of enterprises getting no measurable return on generative AI. OpenAI, valued at $852bn, does not expect a profit before 2030. This is the Pets.com problem at hyperscale: the spending is real, the demand is assumed.

Which crash is the better model

On the evidence, 2000 fits better than 2008, and the fit is uncomfortably close. Valuation is back at the 1999 level: the Shiller CAPE stands at 41 against a dotcom peak of 44 and a long-run median of 17. Concentration is worse than 1999: the top five companies are 30% of the S&P 500 against 17% at the dotcom peak, and the Magnificent Seven are a third of the index. Investor sentiment has already turned: 54% of fund managers surveyed by Bank of America call AI stocks a bubble and name AI the top tail risk. The single-day lesson has been given once, when DeepSeek’s cheap model wiped $589bn dollars from Nvidia on 27 January 2025. And the revenue gap, Bain’s $800bn, is the same gap that killed the dotcoms: infrastructure built for demand that had not arrived.

The differences from 2000 cut both ways. Nvidia trades at roughly 30 times earnings with a 53% net margin, not Cisco’s 201 times. The hyperscalers are profitable incumbents, not two-year-old IPOs. That is the case for a softer landing. But in 2000 the infrastructure was financed by equity that could simply evaporate. This time it is financed by half a trillion dollars of debt.

That is where 2008 re-enters. The analogy with subprime holds on opacity, manufactured demand and who ends up holding the paper. Hyperscalers guarantee the leases of smaller partners, creating contingent liabilities that surface only when called. The ecosystem is, in Robin Wigglesworth’s words, incestuous: the chip vendor invests in the model company, which signs a compute contract with the neocloud, which borrows against that contract to buy the vendor’s chips. It is the 2006 CDO daisy chain with better branding. And the holders are familiar: pension funds and life insurers anchor the bonds.

The analogy with 2008 breaks on the two things that made it systemic. The originators have cash: Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon can write down a trillion dollars of datacentres and still make payroll. And the regulated banks are mostly originating to distribute, not holding.

So the honest model is a hybrid. The hyperscalers get the dotcom outcome: a long, grinding equity drawdown that the companies survive and their shareholders do not enjoy. The neoclouds and their lenders get the Hynix outcome: debt converted to equity, shareholders wiped, assets sold at a fraction of cost. The private credit funds, insurers and retail vehicles in between get the 2008 outcome in miniature, without a taxpayer behind them. A decade-long hangover is the base case.

The cyber short

When the correction arrives, the thing that gets shorted is not a stock. It is the operational resilience of every business that has quietly re-platformed onto these providers.

Your security tooling, your identity provider, your fraud models and your customer-facing assistants increasingly run on inference bought from a neocloud, which bought the GPUs with floating-rate private credit, secured on a contract with a model company that is itself years from profit. In 2008 the question was whether your bank would open on Monday. In this cycle the question is whether the provider holding your data and running your controls is in receivership by Friday, and what the administrator does with the hardware.

Three consequences follow. Distressed providers cut security first, because security is a cost centre and the lender wants cash. Distressed providers get acquired fast, and hostile actors treat a rushed integration as an open door. And distressed providers sell compute cheap. When the 1873 railway bust ended, the tracks were still there and freight became cheap for everyone. When the datacentres are repossessed, inference becomes cheap for everyone, including the people running credential stuffing, deepfake fraud and automated vulnerability discovery against your estate. The attacker’s cost curve falls at exactly the moment your budget does.

Read more about the AI boom

  • A whitepaper from connectivity expert Altnets highlights growing infrastructure pressure, as artificial intelligence demand reshapes the future of digital economies.
  • FinOps practitioners are stepping up to manage AI expenses, optimise token usage and align cost-saving measures with sustainability goals to improve returns from AI investments.
  • AI-powered digital health tools are flooding the market, but providers must look beyond marketing hype and evaluate their vendors to select the right tools for their needs.

The verdict

A 2008-scale crisis needs a single collapsing asset class, leverage inside the institutions that run the plumbing, and paper nobody can price. The AI build-out has the first and the third. It has only partly got the second, because the banks have pushed the risk to private credit, insurers and pensions. A 2000-scale crisis needs stretched valuations, extreme concentration, infrastructure built ahead of revenue and a central bank tightening into it. The AI build-out has all four. My estimate: a correction that impairs a trillion dollars or more of infrastructure and takes the leading indices down by a third to a half is more likely than not by 2029. A Lehman-scale systemic event is roughly one chance in five. Neither number is a reason to relax. The dotcom recovery took 15 years in a far more forgiving world.

The investors who profited in 2008 did one thing differently. They read the collateral before the market did. For a board, the collateral is your supplier chain. The one thing that can be done right now is to commission a financed-supplier concentration review of every AI and cloud provider in your critical path before the next budget cycle, mapped to ISO 27001 supplier and continuity controls, with a costed answer to two questions: what happens if the provider fails, and what happens if the price triples.

Ian Thornton-Trump is fractional CISO at Inversion6.
summary:
The AI build-out will not cause a repeat of the 2008 financial crisis. It is far more likely to cause a repeat of 2000, and that is not the reassurance it sounds like. A dotcom-style bust would still wipe trillions from markets, take a decade or more to recover, and arrive at a moment when the world has less slack to absorb it than it had in either 2000 or 2008.

I watched The Big Short again this week. What struck me was not the collapse.
